metadata.title: Transforming Visual Identity — Raulyn Ladera
metadata.description: Case study on defining the look & feel of the Qik Digital Bank app: visual identity, design principles, and an accessible banking experience.

hero.title: Transforming visual identity into a human, usable experience.

labels.impactSection: The look & feel work didn't start by improving something existing — it started by building a clear, modern, and accessible banking experience from scratch.

challengeParagraphs: With no product, no defined identity, and a white-label brand as the only starting point, I had to design Qik's banking experience from the ground up.

My role began focused on UI, but the lack of a clear visual direction led me to take on the full definition of the look & feel — while the product, the team, and expectations all grew at the same time.
The challenge wasn't just visual: we needed to build an accessible, fast, and simple experience capable of bringing banking to people the traditional financial system had never reached.

summaryCards.label: Key outcome
summaryCards.value: A foundation that evolved into Cobalt Design System

claridad.principlesIntro: The look & feel was built on clear principles:
principlesItems: Visual hierarchy to support reading and navigation.
Contrast and color use to guide attention.
Consistent spacing to create breathing room and clarity.
Repeatable patterns that reduce cognitive friction.
claridad.principlesClosing: I aimed for the app to convey Trust, Modernity, and Simplicity. Qik needed to feel light, accessible, and different from the traditional banking experience.

gridCaptions.loader: A clean, intuitive interface was designed — with one thing always in mind: we're designing a bank.
gridCaptions.animations: Animations and micro-interactions were applied at key moments to reduce anxiety.

gridAlts.loader: Credit card screen in the Qik app

claridad.impactSectionTitle: The look & feel work didn't start by improving something existing — it started by building a clear, modern, and accessible banking experience from scratch.
impactParagraphs: Through visual decisions like typographic hierarchy, contrast, spacing, and repeatable patterns, the product conveyed a sense of trust and simplicity from the very first interaction.
The team began working with greater visual clarity and confidence, while the app started standing out for its cleanliness and coherence.
On social media and in conversations with users, one of the most recurring comments has been how simple, intuitive, and different from traditional banking Qik feels.
claridad.impactLead: More than an interface, design helped create a usable experience where the visual layer naturally guides interaction.
claridad.learningTitle: Seeing the app running for the first time during the launch event is a moment that's hard to describe.
learningParagraphs: I felt a mix of pride and emotion watching something that started as ideas and visual decisions become a real tool that impacts the lives of thousands of people.

Beyond the system or the structure, what fills me most is hearing that Qik is perceived as simple, clear, and well thought out. Knowing that something I designed today is part of Dominican users' daily lives reminds me why I do what I do.
claridad.learningLead: For me, design makes sense when it stops being just a screen and becomes an experience people actually use and value.

metadata.title: Cobalt Design System. — Raulyn Ladera
metadata.description: Case study on designing and documenting Cobalt: a system built on design tokens and atomic design to scale Qik Digital Bank.

hero.title: Atomic design system with design tokens, focused on scalability and consistency.

labels.impactSection: Implementing Cobalt transformed the way the team works.

challengeParagraphs: Qik had a UI Kit, not a system. Every designer made their own decisions, components were rebuilt from scratch, and the language between design and development wasn't aligned.
The result was inconsistency, rework, and limited collaboration across teams.
Scaling the product required building a system — not continuing to work on top of a guideline / UI Kit.
cobalt.systemIntro: Cobalt was designed around two key principles:
principlesItems: Design Tokens as a shared language between design and development.
Atomic Design as a framework for structuring components and patterns at scale.
cobalt.systemClosing: The goal wasn't just visual consistency — it was operational efficiency and technical scalability.

gridCaptions.spacing: Tokens were defined clearly, from color to the values used in gaps.
gridCaptions.colors: Color tokens were created and grouped as global, alias, and specific — enabling themes and modes on demand.

gridAlts.colors: Global, alias, and specific color tokens

cobalt.alignmentSectionTitle: One of the biggest shifts was aligning design and development under a shared language.
alignmentParagraphs: I worked directly with architecture and frontend leads to validate the system's vision — improving implementation speed, product maintainability, and technical clarity.
Today, both teams share concepts like tokens, components, and patterns, which reduced friction and improved communication.

The solid implementation of these foundations is what allowed us to scale the ecosystem to launch new products like Qik Pro, supporting complex visual variations through a native Pro Theme built on token-based architecture.
cobalt.impactSectionTitle: Implementing Cobalt transformed the way the team works.
impactItems: Over 100% increase in design and development team velocity.
Visual consistency and coherence across the app.
Stronger alignment between design and development.
cobalt.impactIntro: Nothing validates the decision to build a design system better than the voice of the technical team that implements it:
cobalt.quote: Without tokens, Qik Pro wouldn't have been possible.
cobalt.learningTitle: Building Cobalt changed my perspective as a designer.
learningParagraphs: I understood that true impact isn't in an isolated interface — it's in creating structures that let design evolve alongside the product and the business.
Today, seeing the system adopted by designers, developers, and leaders across the bank is one of the greatest satisfactions of my career.

metadata.title: Optimizing Figma Architecture — Raulyn Ladera
metadata.description: Case study on DesignOps at Qik: Figma reorganization, standardized technical handoff, and an architecture adopted by the entire design team.

hero.title: Optimizing the team's Figma architecture and technical handoff.

labels.decisionsSection: Designed so anyone can find what they need.
labels.impactSection: The new structure didn't change what we design — it changed how we find it and how we deliver it.

challengeParagraphs: Our Figma was organized by squads (Cafeína Team, Dulcito de Coco, Feeling Box...), but the product had grown and designers were constantly collaborating across different squads.

The result: user stories documented in the wrong files. A story from the Cafeína Team squad ended up in another squad's file simply because the person who executed it belonged to a different team — and finding it later became tedious.
This wasn't just clutter: it cost us speed and discoverability in the design team's day-to-day work.

summaryCards.label: Scope
summaryCards.value: Complete reorganization of Qik in Figma

summaryCards.label: Key outcome
summaryCards.value: Standardized structure adopted by the entire design team

designops.structureIntro: We proposed a five-level architecture adapted to Qik's reality:
structureItems: Organization — all collaborators invited; designers with edit permissions, everyone else with view-only access.
Teams — grouped by actual function: Products, Handover, Marketing, Design System, DesignOps, and Vendors.
Projects — one space per product, core feature, or external collaboration.
Files — specific flows for each product or feature, with naming based on team acronyms and feature names.
Pages — each file divided into UI Team, UX Team, and File Information (handover, cover).
designops.structureClosing: There isn't one "correct" way to structure Figma — the key was adapting the recommended architecture to how Qik actually works.

gridCaptions.organization: Everyone collaborates within Figma, but the Product team maintains the rules that keep the software organized.
gridCaptions.projects: To ensure good organization, we proposed creating projects based on features, products, and teams outside Product Design.

gridAlts.nomenclature: Figma page and file naming conventions

designops.showcaseAlt: Visual structure of Qik Figma files
designops.decisionsSectionTitle: Designed so anyone can find what they need.
decisionsParagraphs: Each file was divided into clear folders: UI Team, UX Team, and the information needed for handoff to development.

On the UI side: explorations, the approved flow (UI Check), prototypes, and a discarded file to preserve the history of decisions. On the UX side: wireframes and benchmarks. And in both, a Handover Info section and a Cover with title, description, and date — so any designer, new or not, can understand the file without having to ask.
designops.impactSectionTitle: The new structure didn't change what we design — it changed how we find it and how we deliver it.
impactItems: Less time lost searching for misplaced files or flows.
Clear collaboration rituals with development: planning, refinement, and evidence centralized in RFD and Jira.
Standardized handover — any designer can pick up a file and understand its status.
A foundation that gets tested, iterated, and adjusted with real team feedback — not a fixed rule.
designops.impactQuote: More than a well-named folder, this gave the team a shared language to work with.
designops.learningTitle: Organizing Figma taught me that structure isn't bureaucracy — it's what gives a growing team real speed.
learningParagraphs: Before this, I thought "organizing files" was a minor task compared to designing screens. Today I know it's the opposite: without an organized foundation, every new screen costs more than it should.
The most valuable part wasn't defining the structure — it was getting the team to adopt it as their natural way of working.
